units.translation: d ' is omitted by two manuscripts, which Meineke in Vindiciae Strabonianae p. 199 plausibly corrected as follows: πρέπουσι μήλων πᾶν τ᾽ Ἐρέχθειον πέδον [the flocks are conspicuous and the whole Erechthean plain], adding this note: "Tantalus says that he occupies the Berecyntian region, where the city Adrastea and Ida and the whole Erechthean plain abound with flocks. By Erechthean plain or land I understand Dardania, which after Dardanus' death Erichthonius held, ὃς δὴ ἀφνειότατος γένετο θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων, τοῦ τρισχίλιαι ἵπποι ἕλος κάτα βουκολέοντο [who was the richest of mortal men, and three thousand horses grazed in his marsh-meadow], as it is in Homer Il. 20, 220. Cf. Analecta Alexandrina p. 357. Erechtheus and Erichthonius are different forms of the same name. Thus the one called by most ὁ πρῶτος ἵππων ἅρμα ζεύξας [the first to yoke horses to a chariot] is called Erechtheus by Themistius Or. 27 p. 337. Cf. Scholia Veneta on Homer Il. 2, 547. Furthermore, by Ἀδραστείας ἕδος [the seat of Adrastea] I do not understand a temple or statue of Adrastea, as Walz in De Nemesi Graeca p. 10 wanted, but the city Adrastea and the adjacent land. Aeschylus spoke thus more than once, who in Pers. 862 called the island of Icarus ἕδος Ικάρου [the seat of Icarus], and other similar expressions. Cf. on Stephanus Byzantius p. 140, 4. Therefore the poet means by the words Ἀδραστείας ἕδος [the seat of Adrastea] the plain of Adrastea, Ἀδραστείας πεδίον [the plain of Adrastea], by which name the city itself and the land were called, see Strabo 13 p. 578 and 588. It is also Aeschylean, which I have restored by a sufficiently certain conjecture, as it seems to me, πρέπουσι [they are conspicuous], which although it is usually said of things that fall under the eyes, nevertheless also
is rightly used here, as is shown among other things by Agamemnon line 321: οἶμαι βοὴν ἄμικτον ἐν πόλει πρέπειν [I think a confused cry is conspicuous in the city].
